# Do men or women have more brothers?

## 0. Answer

Under the stated background assumptions, **neither**: the number of brothers of a
uniformly chosen individual $I$ has *exactly the same conditional distribution*
given that $I$ is male as given that $I$ is female. A fortiori the two
conditional expectations are equal, and this holds whatever the (deliberately
unspecified) distribution of family sizes is.

The intuitive argument — "in each family the girls have at least as many brothers
as the boys, and usually more" — is a genuinely invalid inference. It compares
individuals *within* families, whereas the question asks for an average *over
individuals*, in which families are weighted by their number of boys (for the
men's average) and by their number of girls (for the women's average). Sampling
a person who turns out to be male biases his family towards being boy-rich by
exactly one extra boy in expectation, and this exactly cancels the fact that he
may not count himself.

Sections 1–3 prove the theorem, Section 4 dissects the faulty argument
(including an explicit sex-balanced population in which the argument's premise
holds strictly in every family and yet **men** have more brothers), and
Section 5 delimits the result by showing exactly which hypotheses are doing the
work.

## 1. The model

We formalise the four background assumptions.

**(A1)** The population is a finite set $P$ partitioned into nonempty families
$F_1,\dots,F_N$ with sizes $n_j=|F_j|\ge1$. Write $M=|P|=\sum_{j=1}^N n_j$. The
family structure (the partition, hence all the $n_j$) is *fixed*, i.e.
non-random, and completely arbitrary: this is how we encode "the distribution of
family sizes is deliberately not specified". (Section 3.3 shows that random
family structures reduce to this case.)

**(A2)** Sexes are random: $X_i\in\{\mathsf m,\mathsf f\}$ for $i\in P$, the
variables $(X_i)_{i\in F_j}$ inside each family $F_j$ are mutually independent,
and $\Pr[X_i=\mathsf m]=p$ for **every** $i\in P$, where $p\in(0,1)$ is a single
constant for the whole population. The problem's "half are men and half are
women" is the case $p=\tfrac12$; we keep $p$ general because the conclusion does
not need $p=\tfrac12$. Nothing at all is assumed about dependence *between*
different families (independence across families is used only in Theorem 3).
That $p$ is the *same* for all families is essential and is part of the
hypothesis; see Remark 5.3, which shows that the conclusion genuinely fails
without it.

**(A3)** The individual under study, $I$, is drawn uniformly at random from $P$,
independently of $(X_i)_{i\in P}$. This is what "an individual $I$" means: a
person sampled from the population — *not* a person sampled from a family
sampled from the population, and not a person sampled from some sub-collection
of families (cf. §4.4).

For $i\in P$ let $j(i)$ be the index of $i$'s family and $F(i)=F_{j(i)}$. The
number of brothers of the sampled individual is
$$B \;=\; \#\{\,k\in F(I): k\ne I,\; X_k=\mathsf m\,\}.$$
The clause $k\neq I$ already implements "no man can be his own brother": if
$X_I=\mathsf m$ then $I$ is not counted in $B$.

Finally put
$$b_j=\#\{k\in F_j: X_k=\mathsf m\},\qquad g_j=n_j-b_j ,$$
the numbers of boys and girls in family $j$; by (A2), $b_j\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_j,p)$.

## 2. The main theorem

Let $\mu$ be the *size-biased* family-size law, i.e. the law of $n_{j(I)}$:
$$\mu(\{n\})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j:\,n_j=n} n_j ,\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\mathbb E_\mu[n]=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^N n_j^2 .$$

> **Theorem 1.** Assume (A1)–(A3). Then $B$ is independent of $X_I$. Consequently
> $$\mathcal L\big(B\mid X_I=\mathsf m\big)\;=\;\mathcal L\big(B\mid X_I=\mathsf f\big)\;=\;\mathcal L(B),$$
> this common law being the $\mu$-mixture of binomials
> $$\Pr[B=m]\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{n_j}{M}\binom{n_j-1}{m}p^{m}(1-p)^{\,n_j-1-m},\qquad m\ge 0 ,$$
> and in particular
> $$\mathbb E[B\mid X_I=\mathsf m]\;=\;\mathbb E[B\mid X_I=\mathsf f\,]\;=\;\frac{p}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{N}n_j(n_j-1)\;=\;p\,\big(\mathbb E_\mu[n]-1\big).$$

*Proof.* Fix $i\in P$ and condition on $\{I=i\}$, an event of probability $1/M$
that is independent of the whole sex vector by (A3). On this event
$$B=B_i:=\sum_{k\in F(i)\setminus\{i\}}\mathbf 1\{X_k=\mathsf m\},\qquad X_I=X_i .$$
Both $B_i$ and $X_i$ are functions of the sexes inside the *single* family
$F_{j(i)}$, and by (A2) the variables $(X_k)_{k\in F_{j(i)}}$ are mutually
independent. Hence $X_i$ is independent of the vector
$(X_k)_{k\in F_{j(i)}\setminus\{i\}}$, and therefore of $B_i$, which is a
function of that vector. Moreover $B_i$ is a sum of $n_{j(i)}-1$ independent
$\mathrm{Bern}(p)$ indicators, so $B_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_{j(i)}-1,p)$. Writing
$\pi(\mathsf m)=p$, $\pi(\mathsf f)=1-p$, we get for all $m\ge0$ and
$s\in\{\mathsf m,\mathsf f\}$
$$\Pr\big[B=m,\,X_I=s\,\big|\,I=i\big]
=\Pr[B_i=m]\,\Pr[X_i=s]
=\binom{n_{j(i)}-1}{m}p^m(1-p)^{\,n_{j(i)}-1-m}\cdot\pi(s).$$
The first factor depends on $i$ only through $n_{j(i)}$; the second does not
depend on $i$ at all. Averaging over $i$ with weights $\Pr[I=i]=1/M$ and
grouping the $n_j$ individuals of family $j$ together,
$$\Pr[B=m,\,X_I=s]\;=\;\pi(s)\cdot\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{n_j}{M}\binom{n_j-1}{m}p^m(1-p)^{\,n_j-1-m}.$$
Summing over $m$ gives $\Pr[X_I=s]=\pi(s)$; summing over $s$ gives the asserted
formula for $\Pr[B=m]$. Hence $\Pr[B=m,X_I=s]=\Pr[B=m]\Pr[X_I=s]$, i.e. $B$ and
$X_I$ are independent; since $\pi(s)>0$ for both $s$, both conditional laws
equal $\mathcal L(B)$.

For the mean, $\mathbb E[B\mid I=i]=p\,(n_{j(i)}-1)$, so
$$\mathbb E[B]=\frac1M\sum_{i\in P}p\,(n_{j(i)}-1)=\frac{p}{M}\sum_{j=1}^N n_j(n_j-1)
=p\Big(\frac1M\sum_j n_j^2-1\Big)=p\big(\mathbb E_\mu[n]-1\big).\qquad\blacksquare$$

Note that the proof uses no assumption about the shape of the family-size
profile, no independence between families, and no balance of the sexes; and that
**no family is excluded** — in particular the all-boy and all-girl families are
counted, which (see §4.4) is exactly where the naive argument cheats.

**What depends on the family sizes and what does not.** The *common value*
$p(\mathbb E_\mu[n]-1)$ does depend on the family-size profile — through its
*size-biased* mean, not its ordinary mean. But the *comparison* between the
sexes does not: for every family-size profile and every $p\in(0,1)$, the two
conditional laws coincide exactly. This answers the question as posed: even
knowing nothing whatsoever about the distribution of family sizes, one can
assert that the two expectations are equal.

## 3. Three complements

### 3.1 The population-average ("what would a census show?") formulation

One may object that the question is not about a randomly sampled person but
about the *observed average* number of brothers per man and per woman. Since a
family with $b$ boys and $g$ girls contains $b$ men having $b-1$ brothers each
and $g$ women having $b$ brothers each, those averages are the ratios of sums
$$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}_N=\frac{\sum_{j\le N} b_j(b_j-1)}{\sum_{j\le N} b_j},
\qquad
\overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}_N=\frac{\sum_{j\le N} g_jb_j}{\sum_{j\le N} g_j},$$
defined on the events that the denominators are nonzero. These are ratios of
random variables, not the conditional expectations of Theorem 1, so they require
a separate argument.

> **Theorem 2 (exact, finite population).** For any fixed family-size profile and
> any $p\in(0,1)$,
> $$\frac{\mathbb E\big[\sum_j b_j(b_j-1)\big]}{\mathbb E\big[\sum_j b_j\big]}
> \;=\;\frac{\mathbb E\big[\sum_j g_jb_j\big]}{\mathbb E\big[\sum_j g_j\big]}
> \;=\;\frac{p}{M}\sum_j n_j(n_j-1),$$
> the same value as in Theorem 1.

*Proof.* For $b\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ the second factorial moment is
$\mathbb E[b(b-1)]=n(n-1)p^2$, and
$$\mathbb E[b(n-b)]=n\,\mathbb E[b]-\mathbb E[b^2]=n^2p-\big(np(1-p)+n^2p^2\big)=n(n-1)p(1-p).$$
(Both are exact identities; no term is neglected.) Summing over families,
$\mathbb E\sum_j b_j(b_j-1)=p^2\sum_j n_j(n_j-1)$ and
$\mathbb E\sum_j g_jb_j=p(1-p)\sum_j n_j(n_j-1)$, while $\mathbb E\sum_j b_j=pM$
and $\mathbb E\sum_j g_j=(1-p)M$. Dividing, the factor $p$ cancels in the first
ratio and the factor $p(1-p)/(1-p)=p$ survives in the second; both equal
$\frac{p}{M}\sum_j n_j(n_j-1)$. $\blacksquare$

> **Theorem 3 (large populations).** Let the families be i.i.d.: sizes
> $n_1,n_2,\dots\ge1$ i.i.d. with $\mathbb E[n^2]<\infty$, and, given the sizes,
> all sexes independent $\mathrm{Bern}(p)$. Then almost surely both averages are
> eventually well defined and
> $$\lim_{N\to\infty}\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}_N=\lim_{N\to\infty}\overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}_N
> =\frac{p\,\mathbb E[n(n-1)]}{\mathbb E[n]} .$$

*Proof.* The four sequences $\big(b_j(b_j-1)\big)_j,\ (b_j)_j,\ (g_jb_j)_j,\ (g_j)_j$
are i.i.d. and integrable, each being dominated by $n_j^2$, which has finite
mean. Their means, obtained by averaging the identities in the proof of
Theorem 2 over the random size, are $p^2\mathbb E[n(n-1)]$, $p\,\mathbb E[n]$,
$p(1-p)\mathbb E[n(n-1)]$ and $(1-p)\mathbb E[n]$. By the strong law of large
numbers each empirical mean converges a.s. to its expectation. The two
denominators have strictly positive limits $p\,\mathbb E[n]>0$ and
$(1-p)\mathbb E[n]>0$, so a.s. they are eventually nonzero and the ratios
converge a.s. to
$$\frac{p^2\mathbb E[n(n-1)]}{p\,\mathbb E[n]}\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{p(1-p)\mathbb E[n(n-1)]}{(1-p)\mathbb E[n]},$$
which are the same number. $\blacksquare$

So the tie is not an artefact of one sampling convention: it holds for the
randomly sampled person (Theorem 1), for the ratio of expected totals
(Theorem 2), and as the large-population limit of the observed averages
(Theorem 3).

### 3.2 A minimal illustration

Take one two-person family and $p=\frac12$. Given that $I$ is male, the single
sibling is male with probability $\frac12$, so $\mathbb E[B\mid\mathsf m]=\frac12$;
given that $I$ is female, the same computation gives $\frac12$. Yet in every
mixed family the girl has one brother and the boy has none: the "girls win"
phenomenon is plainly visible family by family, and the averages still tie. The
bookkeeping shows why: over the four equally likely patterns of a two-child
family, the $\{\mathsf{mm}\}$ family contributes *two* men with one brother each
(total $2$ brothers among $4$ men across the four patterns, giving $1/2$), while
$\{\mathsf{mf}\}$ and $\{\mathsf{fm}\}$ each contribute one brotherless man and
one woman with a brother (total $2$ brothers among $4$ women, again $1/2$).
Boy-rich families supply more men to the men's average.

### 3.3 Random family structures

If the partition is itself random but *independent of the sexes*, apply
Theorem 1 conditionally on the partition: the identity
$\mathcal L(B\mid X_I=\mathsf m)=\mathcal L(B\mid X_I=\mathsf f)$ holds for every
realisation of the partition, hence also unconditionally, since a mixture of
pairs of equal conditional laws is a pair of equal laws. Nothing is lost by
taking the sizes fixed. (If the family structure is allowed to depend on the
realised sexes, (A2) is typically destroyed; see Remark 5.2.)

## 4. Where the intuitive argument goes wrong

The argument to be refuted is:

> **(i)** In any single family the girls have at least as many brothers as the
> boys — indeed exactly one more whenever the family contains at least one of
> each sex. **(ii)** Therefore, averaged over the whole population, women have
> more brothers than men.

Step (i) is true and trivial: in a family with $b$ boys and $g$ girls, each girl
has $b$ brothers and each boy has $b-1$. Step (ii) is a non sequitur.

### 4.1 The inference is invalid — it can even reverse

Here is a concrete population in which the premise (i) holds with **strict**
inequality in **every** family, the population is exactly sex-balanced, and yet
**men have strictly more brothers on average**. Take two families
$$F_1=\{\mathsf m,\mathsf m,\mathsf m,\mathsf m,\mathsf f\},\qquad
F_2=\{\mathsf m,\mathsf f,\mathsf f,\mathsf f,\mathsf f\}.$$
There are $5$ men and $5$ women. In $F_1$ the girl has $4$ brothers and each of
the four boys has $3$; in $F_2$ each of the four girls has $1$ brother and the
boy has $0$. So in each family the girls strictly beat the boys. Nevertheless
$$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}=\frac{3+3+3+3+0}{5}=\frac{12}{5}=2.4,
\qquad
\overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}=\frac{4+1+1+1+1}{5}=\frac{8}{5}=1.6 ,$$
so men have $0.8$ more brothers on average. The implication (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii)
is therefore false as a form of reasoning: it is not merely non-strict, it does
not even determine the direction. (A shorter variant, with the premise holding
vacuously in the single-sex families:
$F_1=\{\mathsf m,\mathsf m,\mathsf m\}$, $F_2=\{\mathsf m,\mathsf f\}$,
$F_3=\{\mathsf f,\mathsf f,\mathsf f\}$ gives
$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}=6/4=1.5$ versus $\overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}=1/4$.)

Combined with Theorem 1, the situation is: the per-family observation is true,
the inference from it is invalid, and the correct population-level answer under
the stated assumptions is a dead heat.

### 4.2 Why it is invalid: the two averages use different weights

The per-family statement (i) is the comparison of *within-family* averages
$$\underbrace{\frac{g_jb_j}{g_j}}_{\text{per girl in family }j}=b_j
\;\;\ge\;\;
b_j-1=\underbrace{\frac{b_j(b_j-1)}{b_j}}_{\text{per boy in family }j}.$$
Summing over $j$ does **not** yield the corresponding inequality for the
population averages, because the latter are *ratios of sums*, not sums or
averages of the per-family ratios:
$$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}=\frac{\sum_j b_j\,(b_j-1)}{\sum_j b_j}
=\Big(\text{average of }b_j\text{ with weights }b_j\Big)-1,
\qquad
\overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}=\frac{\sum_j g_j\,b_j}{\sum_j g_j}
=\Big(\text{average of }b_j\text{ with weights }g_j\Big).$$
The men's average weights family $j$ by its number of boys, the women's by its
number of girls. Those weightings are different, and the boy-weighting
systematically favours boy-rich families — precisely the families in which $b_j$
is large. The naive argument tacitly assumes both averages use the same weights,
i.e. that one may compare the two columns family by family and then add up. This
is the structural error behind Simpson's paradox and behind the classical
inspection/size-bias paradoxes ("why are your friends more popular than you").

### 4.3 The exact accounting: the sampling bias is worth exactly one brother

Under the model one can say precisely how much the boy-weighting is worth.

> **Proposition 4.** Let $b(F_I)=b_{j(I)}$ be the number of boys in the sampled
> individual's family. Under (A1)–(A3),
> $$\mathbb E\big[b(F_I)\,\big|\,X_I=\mathsf m\big]\;-\;\mathbb E\big[b(F_I)\,\big|\,X_I=\mathsf f\,\big]\;=\;1 .$$
> More strongly, conditionally on $n_{j(I)}=n$, the number of boys in $I$'s
> family is distributed as $1+\mathrm{Bin}(n-1,p)$ if $I$ is male and as
> $\mathrm{Bin}(n-1,p)$ if $I$ is female.

*Proof.* By definition $b(F_I)=B+\mathbf 1\{X_I=\mathsf m\}$. By Theorem 1, $B$
is independent of $X_I$, whence $\mathbb E[b(F_I)\mid X_I=\mathsf m]=\mathbb E[B]+1$
and $\mathbb E[b(F_I)\mid X_I=\mathsf f]=\mathbb E[B]$. The distributional
statement follows from the display in the proof of Theorem 1, which shows that
conditionally on $I=i$ the pair $(X_i,B_i)$ is independent with
$B_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_{j(i)}-1,p)$. $\blacksquare$

In words: *learning that the sampled person is male raises the expected number of
boys in that person's family by exactly one.* Not because male births cause male
births — by (A2) they are independent — but because a man is more likely to have
been sampled out of a boy-rich family in the first place. The naive argument
correctly spots a deficit of exactly $1$ ("he cannot be his own brother") and
overlooks a surplus of exactly $1$ produced by the sampling. They cancel
identically, which is Theorem 1:
$$\mathbb E[B\mid X_I=\mathsf m]
=\underbrace{\mathbb E[b(F_I)\mid X_I=\mathsf m]}_{=\ \mathbb E[B]+1}
-\underbrace{1}_{\text{not his own brother}}
=\mathbb E[B]=\mathbb E[B\mid X_I=\mathsf f].$$

### 4.4 The tempting repair — restricting to families with both sexes — is illegitimate

The phrase "in any family, say with two girls and one boy" quietly restricts
attention to families containing at least one of each sex, and that restriction
is what manufactures the inequality. Concretely, take all families of size $6$
with $p=\frac12$, all $2^6=64$ sex-patterns equally likely (one family of each
pattern). Since $\sum_{b}\binom6b b=6\cdot2^5=192$,
$\sum_b\binom6b b(b-1)=6\cdot5\cdot2^4=480$ and
$\sum_b\binom6b b(6-b)=6\cdot5\cdot2^4=480$, the full population gives
$$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}=\frac{480}{192}=\frac52=\overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}},$$
a tie, as Theorem 1 requires. But if the two single-sex patterns are discarded,
the men lose the $6$ men of the all-boy family (who had $5$ brothers each, i.e.
$30$ brothers) while the women lose nothing at all (the all-boy family had no
women, and the all-girl family had no brothers to contribute), so
$$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}=\frac{480-30}{192-6}=\frac{450}{186}=\frac{75}{31}\approx2.419,
\qquad
\overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}=\frac{480}{186}=\frac{80}{31}\approx2.581 .$$
The apparent female advantage of $5/31$ is entirely an artefact of deleting the
all-male families — exactly the families that are richest in brothers per man.
Any argument that reasons only about families "with $n$ girls and $m$ boys,
$n,m\ge1$" has therefore assumed its conclusion.

## 5. Three remarks delimiting the result

### 5.1 If the number of men is *exactly* half, women do win — by $O(1/M)$

Assumption (A2) makes the sexes independent, so the number of men is only
*approximately* $M/2$. Consider instead the alternative idealisation in which
$M$ is even and exactly $M/2$ individuals are men, the set of men being a
uniformly random $M/2$-subset of $P$ (the sexes are then exchangeable but not
independent), with $I$ uniform and independent as before.

> **Proposition 5.** In this exact-balance model,
> $$\mathbb E[B\mid X_I=\mathsf f\,]-\mathbb E[B\mid X_I=\mathsf m]
> =\frac{1}{M(M-1)}\sum_{j=1}^N n_j(n_j-1)\;\;\in\;\;\Big[0,\ \frac{\max_j n_j-1}{M-1}\Big].$$

*Proof.* $I$ is uniform and independent of the assignment, and the assignment is
exchangeable, so $\Pr[I=i\mid X_I=s]=\Pr[I=i]=1/M$ for every $i$ and $s$;
conditioning on the sex therefore does not change the law of $I$'s family size.
Condition on $I=i$ and $X_i=\mathsf m$. By exchangeability the remaining $M-1$
individuals carry a uniformly random arrangement of $M/2-1$ men, so the number of
men among $i$'s $n_{j(i)}-1$ family-mates is hypergeometric with mean
$(n_{j(i)}-1)\frac{M/2-1}{M-1}$. Given $X_i=\mathsf f$ the same computation gives
$(n_{j(i)}-1)\frac{M/2}{M-1}$. The difference is $\frac{n_{j(i)}-1}{M-1}$, and
averaging over $i$ with weights $1/M$ gives
$\frac{1}{M(M-1)}\sum_j n_j(n_j-1)$. Finally
$\sum_j n_j(n_j-1)\le(\max_j n_j-1)\sum_j n_j=(\max_j n_j-1)M$. $\blacksquare$

So under exact balance the questioner's instinct is literally correct, but the
advantage is of order $\max_j n_j/M$: for a world population of billions with
bounded family sizes it is about $10^{-9}$ of a brother — not the "usually more"
that the per-family argument suggests. The heuristic gets the sign right for the
wrong reason and the magnitude wrong by nine orders of magnitude. Under the
independence hypothesis actually stated in the problem, even that residue
disappears and the answer is an exact tie.

### 5.2 If the family composition reacts to the sexes, women can win outright

Within-family independence is essential. Suppose parents follow the stopping
rule "keep having children until a boy is born, then stop". Every family then
consists of $k-1$ girls followed by one boy $(k\ge1)$; with fair coins the
expected family size is $2$ and there is exactly one boy per family, so the
population is still half male in expectation. But now **every man has $0$
brothers and every woman has exactly $1$**, so women have strictly more — by a
full brother. Of course (A2) fails here: within such a family the sexes are far
from independent (the position of the unique boy is determined by the family
size). This shows that it is assumption (A2), not any intuition about
self-exclusion, that drives the tie.

### 5.3 A *common* $p$ across families is also essential

Suppose the sexes are independent *within* each family but the boy-probability
varies from family to family — say family $j$ has its own $p_j$, so that (A2)
holds only conditionally on the family's type, and the marginal
$\Pr[X_i=\mathsf m]$ is no longer a single constant $p$ (unconditionally, sexes
within a family are then positively correlated, so the stated hypothesis 4 fails
in its unconditional reading). Theorem 1 breaks down, because conditioning on
$X_I=\mathsf m$ then biases the sampled family not only towards large families
but also towards boy-prone *types*. Both directions are possible, so no general
statement survives:

* **Men ahead.** Half the families have $n=6$ children with $p=\tfrac18$, half
  have $n=6$ children with $p=\tfrac78$. The population is exactly half male
  ($\mathbb E[b]=\mathbb E[g]=3$ per family). With
  $\mathbb E[b(b-1)]=\tfrac12\cdot30\cdot(\tfrac1{64}+\tfrac{49}{64})=\tfrac{375}{32}$
  and $\mathbb E[b(n-b)]=30\cdot\tfrac{7}{64}=\tfrac{105}{32}$, Theorem 2's
  computation gives
  $$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}=\frac{375/32}{3}=\frac{125}{32}\approx3.91,
  \qquad \overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}=\frac{105/32}{3}=\frac{35}{32}\approx1.09 .$$
* **Women ahead.** Two thirds of the families have $n=2$ with $p=\tfrac56$ and
  one third have $n=8$ with $p=\tfrac13$; again the population is exactly half
  male ($\mathbb E[b]=\mathbb E[g]=2$), and
  $$\overline B^{\,\mathrm{men}}=\frac{\mathbb E[b(b-1)]}{\mathbb E[b]}=\frac{3}{2},
  \qquad
  \overline B^{\,\mathrm{women}}=\frac{\mathbb E[b(n-b)]}{\mathbb E[g]}=\frac{13/3}{2}=\frac{13}{6}\approx2.17 .$$

Hence heterogeneity in the boy-probability does not favour either sex in
general; which sex comes out ahead depends on how the boy-propensity is
correlated with family size. In particular one must not claim that
family-to-family heterogeneity implies that men have more brothers. Under the
problem's hypotheses — a single $p$, independence within families — the answer
is the exact tie of Theorem 1.

## 6. Summary

* Under (A1)–(A3) the number of brothers of a randomly sampled individual is
  **independent of that individual's sex** (Theorem 1). Men and women therefore
  have the same distribution — hence the same mean, median and variance — of
  number of brothers, for every family-size profile and every sex ratio
  $p\in(0,1)$. The common expectation is $p\,(\mathbb E_\mu[n]-1)$, where $\mu$
  is the size-biased family-size law. The same value is obtained as the ratio of
  expected totals (Theorem 2) and as the almost-sure limit of the observed
  averages in a large population (Theorem 3).
* The "girls have more brothers in every family" argument is invalid because the
  two population averages are weighted averages over families with *different*
  weights ($b_j$ for men, $g_j$ for women) (§4.2). An explicit sex-balanced
  population in which the premise holds strictly in every family while men have
  strictly more brothers on average shows that the inference carries no force at
  all (§4.1), and restricting attention to families containing both sexes — the
  usual implicit move — manufactures the female advantage by deleting exactly the
  all-boy families (§4.4).
* Quantitatively, conditioning on the sampled individual being male inflates the
  expected number of boys in the family by exactly $1$, precisely offsetting the
  fact that he is not his own brother (Proposition 4).
* The tie is sharp, not robust: under exact (rather than independent) sex balance
  women lead by $\frac{1}{M(M-1)}\sum_j n_j(n_j-1)=O(\max_j n_j/M)$ (§5.1);
  under sex-dependent stopping rules women can lead by a full brother (§5.2);
  and under family-to-family heterogeneity of the boy-probability either sex can
  lead (§5.3).
